answer.rationale: Finance requires an 18% spend cut and the incumbent refuses to reopen price this cycle, so renewing with them cannot satisfy the primary objective on its own. Memory c2 (verified) records that switching primary supply to the low-cost vendor last year sharply reduced unit cost, onboarding was quick, and invoicing stayed accurate. That empirical base materially reduces the risk of switching now. The incumbent's refusal also shifts the negotiation payoff (memory c4) toward an external option rather than another internal round. Switching also lets me avoid running the line at 94% with no buffer against a single-source failure. The other directions are weaker: renewing preserves stability but fails the cost mandate; adding a second source is the right pattern when the primary is constrained and I need dual sourcing (memory c3), but here the cost mandate is binding and the cycle has only one slot — a second source does not itself deliver the 18% cut; negotiating is foreclosed by the incumbent's stated refusal; deferring (memory c5) is useful for non-critical renewals, but a 14-day, non-auto-renewing primary supply contract with a constrained line is not non-critical. To keep delivery risk low while honoring the single-decision constraint, I would stage the switch as a small, guarded test rather than a full cutover.
